The French DPA (CNIL) held that using an unprotected URL address to share documents containing personal data violates Article 32 GDPR. Retaining personal data of an applicant for a lease after another applicant has been selected also violates Article 5(1)(e) GDPR.

The authority investigated, on its own initiative, the entry procedure at festivals run by Sziget, where visitors' ID documents were scanned and photos and recordings taken. For 2016 to 24 May 2018 (Infotv.) it found no proper legal basis, breach of purpose limitation and inadequate prior information, but imposed no fine because the company was an SME and the practice had ended. For the period from 25 May 2018 (GDPR) it found an invalid legal basis and breaches of purpose limitation and data minimisation. It fined the company HUF 30,000,000, ordered it to bring its practice into line with the GDPR and ordered publication of the decision.

The DPA fined a controller €107,000 for repeatedly sending unsolicited marketing communications without the data subject's consent. The controller bore liability even though it was a third-party who sent the communications using their own database.

The complainant was refused a subscription contract because Respondent 1 said he had unpaid debts from earlier contracts, which it had assigned to Respondent 2. The contracts had been transferred into his name by phone by a person using his birth data and ID number but giving different mothers' names. Respondent 1 wrongly told him it no longer held his data and refused access, and it kept four different mother's names for him. Respondent 2 processed his data on the wrong legal basis (contract performance). The Authority found breaches of access, transparency, accuracy and accountability by Respondent 1 and of legal basis and accountability by Respondent 2. It fined them HUF 2,000,000 and HUF 1,000,000, ordered them to prove a legitimate interest or stop, restricted processing in the meantime, and rejected the requests for erasure and a processing ban.

Category:Article 4(1) GDPR Category:2019 The President of the Personal Data Protection Office in Poland (UODO) imposed the first fine in the amount of over PLN 943 000 for the failure to fulfil the information obligation.
Portuguese DPA rules that not posting signage about CCTV footage collection in covered areas represents a breach of the controller's information duties under article 13 GDPR

In 2019, the Norwegian DPA fined a municipality about €158,315 (NOK 1,600,000) for lacking security measures, as discovered by a 12 year old pupil at the school. The school pressed charges against the pupil, but withdrew them after massive media pressure.

A law firm article reports that Malta's data protection commissioner fined the Lands Authority EUR 5,000 on 18 February 2019. The Authority's website lacked appropriate security measures, so over 10 GB of personal data, mostly sensitive and including correspondence with individuals, could be found through a simple Google search. The Authority did not appeal and has begun penetration testing and moved its data to servers run by the Malta Information Technology Agency. The article is a secondary commentary, not the decision itself, and cites no GDPR articles.
Portuguese DPA rules that phone call recordings must be made available to the data subject upon his/her request under article 15 GDPR.

The UK DPA (ICO) fined Leave.EU, the Brexit campaign group, and Eldon Insurance, an insurance company, a total of approximately €140,900 (GBP 120,000) for serious breaches of the PECR and sending nearly 300,000 emails to Eldon customers with a Leave.EU newsletter.

The CNIL imposed a record fine of €50 million on Google for several violations of GDPR including processing personal data without a lawful basis, violating the free consent principle and the transparent information principle.

This is a law firm's news article, not the decision itself. A patient complained that a State Hospital did not satisfy her request for access to her medical file because the file could not be located. After investigating, the Cypriot Commissioner imposed an administrative fine of EUR 5,000 on the hospital. The article also reports a separate EUR 10,000 fine on a newspaper for publishing the names and pictures of police officers; that case is not part of this record.

A law firm's news article reports two separate decisions of the Cyprus data protection Commissioner. One fined a State Hospital EUR 5,000 for failing to satisfy a patient's access request because her medical file could not be located. In the other, a newspaper was fined EUR 10,000 for publishing, in print and online, the names and pictures of two police officers, and a photograph of a third. The Commissioner held that the aim could be reached with initials, blurred faces or distant photographs, and weighed EU Court of Justice case law on freedom of expression versus privacy.

A heise online article reports that the Hamburg data protection authority issued a fine notice on 17 December 2018 against a small shipping company, Kolibri Image. The company let a postal service intermediary process customer data without a data processing agreement and refused, even after advice from the Hessian authority, to draw one up. Hamburg found a breach of Art. 28(3) GDPR and set a fine of EUR 5,000 plus EUR 250 fees, treating the conduct as intentional. The company's representative said he would object to the notice.

The Baden-Württemberg DPA holds, that by storing passwords in plain text, the company knowingly violated its obligation to ensure data security when processing personal data in accordance with Art. 32(1)a GDPR.
Portuguese DPA determines generalized access to patient records within a hospital breaches the minimization, integrity and confidentiality principles.

The DSB fined a betting store € 5.280 for video surveillance (CCTV) that was recording a wide area in front of the location, without protocols of the usage, without deletion within 72 hours and without public marking of the video surveillance.
The Dutch DPA fined €150,000/month (until requirements are met) the employer portal UWV, handling employee health data, due to insufficiently secure access control to its portal.

The DSB found that a fee of €30 for a copy of historic bank transaction data, that is not available via online banking anymore, violates the right to access under Article 15 GDPR. GDPR is also applicable to cases that were brought under Directive 95/46 but were pending before the DPA on 25. 5. 2018.

Category:Article 12(5) GDPR The DSB issued a decision related to the righ to be forgotten: to exercise this right, the controller may not require more data than the ones previously asked to the data subject.
The Spanish DPA closed a procedure against the proprietor of a false camera installed in a public space because they did not process any personal data.

<!--Here the main article starts--> The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) decided not to take further actions on Google, LLC (Google Spain, S.L.) and Facebook Spain, S.L. as data controllers for the non-compliance with the right to be forgotten of a Spanish citizen, as per Article 17 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA referred a case to the Irish DPA regarding Facebook transfers of data to third parties. The Irish DPA rejected the case, since Ireland has not implemented Article 80(2) GDPR and the consumer organisation that brought the claim in Spain could therefore not act without an individual mandate.

The Spanish DPA found that an access request was abusive, taking into account the context and the background of the relationship between the data subject and the controller. The data subject had previously filed various claims and lawsuits against the controller in other fields of law.
The Spanish DPA considered that the use of drones by the municipality of Fuenlabrada (Spain) for vehicle traffic control purposes was compliant with GDPR.

The Spanish DPA was not able to launch a sanction procedure because the ICO did not send any information following their cooperation request in the IMI, despite having accepted the case. After Brexit, the Spanish authority decided to archive the case.

The Spanish DPA held that the monitoring of news and social networks by the Directorate for National Security and the Spanish police forces did not violate any data protection regulation, since no personal data had been processed.

The Spanish DPA confirmed that the use of a thermal camera by private security guards to detect individuals' temperatures does does not fall under the scope of the GDPR when there is no further processing of the data shown by the camera, and the persons are not asked to identify themselves.

The Spanish DPA concluded that the use of a thermal camera to verify if users of a service have a higher temperature than a certain threshold, in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, does not fall under the scope of the GDPR when there is no further storing, processing or any operation on the data shown by the camera, and the persons are not asked to identify themselves.

<!--Here the main article starts--> The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) decided not to take further actions on Telefónica as data controller for a possible personal data breach affecting confidentiality, as per Article 32 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA decided not to fine a football club that suffered a data breach because it had implemented adequate security measures and was diligent in mitigating the breach's consequences and reporting it to the authority.

The Spanish DPA considered that the software developer of the interactive, real-location game 'Pokemon Go', had implemented adequate measures to mitigate the risks stemming from the fact malicious users could fake their location, and misuse the location data of other users.
The Spanish DPA established that the parameters of a productivity calculation is not personal data and is therefore not subject to the right to rectification.
The Spanish DPA ordered a controller to comply with a data subject's access request, either by providing the requested information or by explaining why it did not comply with the request.
The Spanish DPA dismissed a complaint about the use of surveillance camera in public spaces. The equipment was never put into use, so there was no processing of personal data.

The Spanish DPA sanctioned a processor for violating GDPR Articles 28(2) and 28(3). This was despite the fact that no written contract existed between the processor and the subprocessors and the controller had not been told of the subprocessors' involvement in data processing activities.

The Spanish DPA handled a personal data breach notified by the Fundación Sociedad Científica de Oncología Médica (FSOM), the foundation behind the study, after a cyber incident at its processor, a CRO, affected study participants' contact and health data. The DPA found that the controller lacked appropriate technical and organisational measures, and proposed a fine of EUR 70,000 under Article 5(1)(f) GDPR. The controller admitted liability, paid voluntarily and waived administrative appeals, so two cumulative 20% reductions brought the fine to EUR 42,000, and it was ordered to demonstrate the measures within three months.

The DPA fined Vodafone €1,050,000 for the failure to implement adequate security measures, allowing the unlawful registration of an additional phone line and the disclosure of duplicate invoices to third parties.
The DPA fined a newspaper €20,000 for publishing an identifiable video of an assault victim and a minor assailant, since their identification was unnecessary for reporting the incident.

The DPA held that a municipality violated the principle of confidentiality after examination papers from an employment-training were disposed in the general waste instead of being destroyed. This allowed for access to the information by third parties.

A former employee complained that his employer had installed cameras that record sound as well as images in work areas, and that the recordings were the sole basis for a disciplinary dismissal procedure. The company confirmed that the system records audio and said this was needed because of a burglary and to document its dispute with the employee. The AEPD held that recording audio in the workplace is intrusive and disproportionate, because testimony from colleagues or the video images alone would have been enough. It fined the company EUR 4,000 for breaching the data minimisation principle (Article 5(1)(c) GDPR) and ordered it to disable the audio mode within one month. The company filed no submissions, so the initiation agreement was treated as the resolution proposal.

A Dutch complainant asked Michael Page, part of PageGroup, for access to her data and was first asked for excessive identity documents. The Dutch authority transferred the complaint to the AEPD as lead authority. The AEPD found that the rights-handling procedure run by the Spanish entity PAGE GROUP EUROPE, S.L. breached Article 12 and the data minimisation principle of Article 5(1)(c) GDPR, and proposed fines of EUR 50,000 and EUR 250,000. The company paid EUR 240,000 voluntarily with the 20% reduction, so the proceedings were declared terminated. No further measures were ordered because the company had adopted a new procedure.

The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) decided not to take further actions on Sound Soul, S.L. as data controller for the possible non-compliance with the data minimisation principle, as per Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined €5,000 (reduced to €3,000) Abanca Corporación Bancaria for using unnecessary cookies on their website before obtaining the consent of the user.

The AEPD issued a reprimand to the Ministry of internal affairs due to their misuse of surveillance cameras in a police station. The controller did not inform about the specific purposes of the surveillances cameras which were used for the employees' monitoring and, thus, breached the principle of purpose limitation.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a warning on an association for the protection of prison workers for publishing personal data without consent on Twitter.
The Spanish Data Protection Agency sanctioned the Municipality of El Espinar with a warning for violating GDPR by publicly disclosing personal data in electoral board lists.

The Spanish DPA held that where an employee had signed an image rights transfer agreement with their employer, prior to the display of an advertisement banner using the employee's image, this could be considered as a legal basis for data processing.

The AEPD issued a reprimand to the Directorate-General of the Spanish Civil Guard for a lack of transparency. The data controller did not provide information to the data subjects who filled out the travel permit form with their personal data, as required by Article 13 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA (AEDP) fined FURNISHYOURSPACE SL €3,000 for infringing the Spanish Law regulating cookies after an investigation launched due to a complaint referred by the Berlin DPA, for offering unclear information and not giving the option of rejecting the cookies.
The Spanish DPA issued a warning to Iberia Líneas Aéreas de España for not informing their workers in accordance with Article 13 GDPR regarding a fingerprint clock-in system.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) issued a warning to a pub for recording and disseminating the image of its customers on their social networks without a legal basis.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) decided to early finish the sanction procedure against the company Bodegas Dinastía, S.L. (the defendant) for the infringement of its information duties related to cookies, as per Article 22(2) of the Spanish Law on Information Society Services (LSSI) — amongst others, the Spanish law regulating cookies — and Article 13 of the GDPR. The defendant agreed to an early settlement of the case by paying a reduced fine (1,600 €) out of the total envisaged by the AEPD in case of ascertained violation (2,000 €).
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) warned a Home Owners' Association for an infringement of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, due to the disclosing of personal data in a debtors list.

The Agencia Española de Protección de Datos filed a case brought by ms. A.A.A against mr. B.B.B in which the applicant denounced that the respondent had installed a video surveillance system with an alleged focus on the complainant's house, infringing article 5(3) GDPR which enshrines the principle of data minimisation.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined Telefónica €15,000 for failing to respond to a customer's objection under Article 21 GDPR, who asked several times to stop receiving advertising e-mails.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) closed a procedure against a website after verifying that it only automatically installed necessary cookies without users’ consent.
The AEPD warned the Asturian Handball Federation for not having appointed a DPO and not having complied with Article 13 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) decided to impose a fine up to €30,000 on Twitter International Company (Twitter Spain, S.L.) for the infringement of its information duties related to cookies, as per Article 22(2) of the Spanish Law on Information Society Services (LSSI) —this is the Spanish law regulating cookies, connected to Article 13 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA fined Orange €50,000 (reduced to €30,000) for processing personal data without a valid legal basis, since processing was based on a fraudulent telephone portability contract. The DPA stated that Orange did not have an adequate identity verification system for portability requests.
The Spanish DPA issued a reprimand against the municipality of Ayuntamiento de Molina de Segura for lacking a DPO.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) issued a warning to the city Council of Burgos for not having appointed a data protection officer, thus breaching Article 37 GDPR.
The Spanish DPA issued a warning to the former worker of a business that processed personal data of their clients from a previous employment relationship without any legitimate basis.

<!--Here the main article starts--> The claimant filed a complaint with the AEPD against the political party Partido Socialista Obrero Español (PSOE) for failing respect his right to object to the processing of information as they sent him political advertisement by email.
The DPA fined the Spanish Soccer Federation €100,000 for requesting more documents than required in the course of its registration procedure, thus violating the principle of data minimisation.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) found that the Regionalist Party of Aragon (PAR) violated Article 21 GDPR by continuing to send an individual unsolicited political canvassing materials after she had exercised her right to reject.
The AEPD found that the Socialist Party of Catalonia (PSC-PSOE) violated Article 21 GDPR due to unsolicited political propaganda sent after the data subject exercised his right to object.
The Spanish DPA warned a City Council for infringing the integrity and confidentiality principle by publishing personal data related to a public grant procedure.

The AEPD issued a reprimand to the Spanish far-right political party VOX. The data controller had sent an email without blind copying, to the members of that political party, infringing Article 5(1)(f) GDPR (integrity and confidentiality principle).
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) warned a Municipality for failing to meet its information obligations to its employees regarding the placement of video surveillance cameras that also record audio.
The Spanish DPA fined a website €3000 for installing third-party cookies without the user's consent, as well as for not informing the user about the purpose of such cookies.

The APED fined 2.500 € a data controller for sending advertisement email without blind carbon copy (Bcc) the email recipients. By disclosing the email addresses of the recipient, the company violated the principle of integrity and confidentiality – Article 5(1)(f) GDPR-.
The Spanish DPA issued a warning to a minor that recorded a video while assaulting another minor, together with a group of others, and subsequently posted it on Instagram.
The AEPD issued a Spanish City Council with a warning of an infringement of Article 5(1)(c) pursuant to Article 83(5) over installed surveillance cameras in the City Hall.

The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) decided to impose a minor warning on a Spanish citizen (the defendant) for the non-adequate installation of a video surveillance system allegedly pointing to the common swimming pool of the housing association, and the consequent infringement of the data minimisation principle related, as per Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) issued a reprimand to a Spanish religious brotherhood (sacramental y penitencial cofradía de nuestro padre jesús sacramentado y maría santísima de la piedad, amparo de los leoneses) for unlawfully processing personal data of its members.
The Spanish DPA held that, for an access request to be valid, it should be done through the appropriate channel (in this case, the DPO), and should be properly documented.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) admitted a claim against the Asturias Healthcare System for not attending a data subject's access request to medical data.

The Spanish DPA decided that, in light of an access request, the controller needs to inform the data subject about whether it has transferred their data to third parties and to whom, even if the controller does not hold any data itself.

The Spanish DPA decided to archive a 'right to be forgotten' case, stating that the data subject did not have any interests which overrode the rights to freedom of speech and information of the newspaper. The search result that the data subject wished to de-list was of public relevance, was not obsolete, and was not proven to be incorrect.

<!--Here the main article starts--> The AEPD received a complaint from a citizen who tried to exercise the right to erasure pursuant to Article 17 GDPR. The controller did not respond to the request. As such, the AEDP notified the controller of responding within ten business days with either a confirmation of the data being deleted or a reasoning for not deleting the data.

The DPA held that automatically refusing to disclose the identity of persons who accessed medical records was incompatible with the enhanced transparency required in the healthcare context, in violation of Article 15 GDPR. It ordered the controller to grant access or provide a properly reasoned refusal.

A complainant and relatives were required by their bank's branch to hand over a full notarial inheritance deed, including information about third parties, to process the estate of a deceased account co-holder. The AEPD found that CaixaBank breached data protection by design (Art. 25 GDPR) and failed to give Art. 13 information. It proposed fines of EUR 500,000 and EUR 10,000 and closed the Art. 30 charge. CaixaBank paid voluntarily, without admitting liability, and obtained a 20% reduction, so the final fine was EUR 408,000. The AEPD ended the procedure and ordered corrective measures within six months.
The DPA fined a notary €2,000 for disclosing protected cadastral data, including a data subject’s name and address, to a client without a legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR.
The DPA found that a public authority’s mobile app collected more personal data than necessary, including IP addresses and device data, in violation of principle of data minimisation.

The DPA fined a controller RON 26,294 (€5,000) for failing to implement adequate security measures, which led to a breach affecting the confidentiality and availability of personal data following a cyberattack.
The Romanian DPA fined a medical clinic approximately €2.000 after it unlawfully processed and disclosed a patient's health data to another controller.

The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) held that intent is not a criterium to assess processing and that mistakenly sending an e-mail does not necessarily constitute a data breach as a human error does not always mean the technical and organisational measures are not adequate. Finally, the DPA held that merely receiving an e-mail is not processing.

<!--Here the main article starts--> The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) reaffirms the importance of the data subjects’ rights, especially when the data processing involves special categories of personal data as understood by Article 9 GDPR.

The DPA fined a public-sector group €5,250 for unlawfully disclosing an employee's audio recording to recipients that were in copy of the access request. The controller should have ensured the data subject intended to provide the recording to such recipients.

The Croatian Personal Data Protection Agency (AZOP) has decided that Raiffeisen bank was in violation of the GDPR by asking its clients to pay approx. 200 HRK (approx. 30 EUR) for delivering documentation regarding a home loan. The client needed it to initiate proceedings for reimbursement of overcharged debt. The Bank says it will not give up its current practice.
The DPA held that the operator of a retail store lawfully operated a CCTV system and reviewed a recording after a data subject accused the store’s staff of coercion.
The Danish DPA ruled that the controller must answer clearly if there are automated decisions made against the data subject in the context of an access requests, to comply with Article 15(1)(h) GDPR.

<!--Here the main article starts-->The Danish Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) issued a reprimand concerning the use of an acquired development and testing environment without implementing the appropriate security measures as required by Article 32 GDPR. The server was internally classified as an internal developer box and was not under review for the ordinary patching and security policy.
The Danish DPA expressed criticism about a system used by multiple municipalities following a security incident that exposed the employment-related information of about 1.5 million citizens.

The Danish DPA published a decision in which it expressed severe criticism of Epic Booking for publishing and keeping extensive number of pictures of children and young people on its Facebook page without having a valid lawful basis for processing. The DPA found that the company failed to provide the data subjects with all information pursuant to Article 13 GDPR as well as to set a retention period for the personal data.

<!--Here the main article starts--> The Danish Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) decided on two similar cases regarding the notification requirements in the case of a personal data breach, 2019-441-1581 and 2019-441-1578. Both cases regarded insufficient access controls on a web based reporting service. In both cases, the information regarding customers’ orders were freely available online. Datatilsynet emphasized that the decision to not inform data subjects about a personal data breach pursuant to Article 34 was based on an insufficient assessment.

<!--Here the main article starts--> The Danish Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) decided on two similar cases regarding the notification requirements in the case of a personal data breach, 2019-441-1581 and 2019-441-1578. Both cases regarded insufficient access controls on a web based reporting service. In both cases, the information regarding customers’ orders were freely available online. The Danish DPA emphasized that the decision to not inform data subjects about a personal data breach pursuant to Article 34 was based on an insufficient assessment. The controller was ordered to notify the affected data subjects.

The Danish DPA (Datatilsynet) found itself incompetent to assess which of the different legal grounds applicable to an access request is the most beneficial for the complainant, in a case where a prison officer requested access to all documents that mentioned his name.

The Danish DPA (Datatilsynet) held that a website's cookie consent mechanism did not gather valid consent, as it only displayed a "Allow all cookies" button. Not clicking the button and continuing to use the website was seen as consent to marketing cookies, which the DPA confirmed was illegal. The DPA also considered the new design of the website's consent mechanism and encouraged the controller to reconsider the option it chose.

The Danish DPA reprimanded the company Jo:ga ApS for using its members' date of birth as a permanent password and failing to implement appropriate security measures such as access restrictions after unsuccessful login attempts.

The Danish DPA (Datatilsynet) found the Family Court in violation of Articles 32(1) and 28(3) due to excessive human and technical errors resulting in leakage of personal data - including many with address protection - and incomplete/lacking data processor agreements.

THE EUROPEAN DATA PROTECTION BOARD Whereas: (1) The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) is an independent body with legal personality, responsible for ensuring the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). (2) The EDPB succeeds the Article 29 Working party set up under Article 29 of Directive 95/46/EC. It is composed of the Member States data protection authorities and the EDPS. (3) The GDPR enters into application today, 25 May 2018, while the Directive 95/46/EC is repealed with effect from today. (4) The Article 29 Working Party has committed itself and adopted in the last two years guidelines and other documents on various aspects of the GDPR, contributing thus to the consistent application of the GDPR. The Article 29 Working Party has consulted interested parties, where appropriate. Acknowledges the continuity of the work provided by the predecessor Article 29 Working Party. Without prejudice to any future revision as appropriate, it endorses the Article 29 Working Party documents as following: 1. Guidelines on consent under Regulation 2016/679, WP259 rev.01 2. The AEPD fined a gas distribution company €12,000 for a violation of Article 5(1)(f) of the GDPR.

A supermarket customer submitted a request via Mercadona's website to access security camera footage following an accident, aiming to substantiate a damages claim. Mercadona failed to respond within one month, later claiming it had not received the request and that the recordings were erased due to an internal human error. The Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) established that Mercadona breached Articles 12 and 15 GDPR by failing to handle the data subject's access request within the statutory timeframe, as well as Article 6 GDPR for unlawful processing. Rejecting Mercadona's arguments regarding early termination reductions under administrative law, the AEPD imposed fines totaling EUR 170,000 (EUR 70,000 for Articles 12/15 and EUR 100,000 for Article 6) and ordered the company to bring its practices into compliance within one month.

The Spanish DPA investigated Google LLC after complaints about Google passing personal data contained in content-removal requests to the Lumen Project website (lumendatabase.org). It found an infringement of Article 6 GDPR (no legal basis) and of Article 17 GDPR (right to erasure), and fined Google EUR 5,000,000 for each, EUR 10,000,000 in total. It also ordered Google to bring its processing operations and the procedures for exercising the right into line with data protection law within six months.
An association that disclosed personal data of one of its members in a Whatsapp group was fined €3,000 for violating Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR.

A customer complained to the Bavarian authority that Openbank, for anti-money-laundering checks, asked him to prove the origin of funds but offered no secure channel, only ordinary unencrypted email. The complaint was passed to the AEPD as lead authority. The AEPD found that Openbank had breached Article 25 GDPR (data protection by design) and Article 32 GDPR (security of processing), as its risk assessment did not cover this document collection and no secure channel existed from May 2018 to October 2022. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,500,000 for Article 25 and EUR 1,000,000 for Article 32, EUR 2,500,000 in total.

The Spanish DPA sanctioned Orange Espagne after fraudulent SIM card duplicates were issued, enabling identity theft and fraudulent banking activity. It found that Orange had processed personal data without a lawful basis (Article 6) and had not put in place data protection by design measures (Article 25). It imposed EUR 200,000 for the Article 6 infringement and EUR 1,000,000 for the Article 25 infringement, and ordered Orange to report within six months the measures taken to ensure duplicate requests come from the line holder. Orange's arguments on criminal prejudicial issues, concurrent infringements, strict liability and proportionality were rejected.
A DPA imposed two fines totalling €45,000,000 on Vodafone for security deficiencies and failure to adequately review and monitor partner agencies working on its behalf.

Amadeus, a global distribution system (GDS) provider for the travel industry, used travellers' booking data in a pilot project that ran from 15 March to 15 June 2022. Millions of people were affected. They were not informed as Article 14 GDPR requires, and the processing had no valid legal basis under Article 6 GDPR. The AEPD proposed a fine of EUR 9,000,000 for each infringement, EUR 18,000,000 in total. Amadeus paid voluntarily without admitting responsibility, which gave a 20% reduction to EUR 14,400,000. The proceedings ended on that payment, and Amadeus waived its administrative appeal.

A customer filed a complaint with the Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) after an unauthorized third party fraudulently obtained a duplicate SIM card at a retail store. The AEPD determined that Xfera Móviles (Yoigo) acted with gross negligence by failing to follow its established identity verification procedures, thereby processing personal data without a valid legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR. Taking into account the company's annual turnover and a previous fine for a similar SIM swapping incident, the regulator imposed a fine of EUR 200,000. Additionally, Xfera was ordered to demonstrate within six months the adoption of measures to prevent similar incidents and guarantee lawful data processing.

On 30 May 2023, Vodafone España notified the Spanish data protection authority of a personal data breach resulting from a ransomware attack on a customer service data processor. The incident compromised unencrypted MSISDNs and landline telephone numbers of 486,768 individual customers as well as contact telephone numbers of 14,571 corporate authorized representatives. The AEPD found that Vodafone failed to ensure appropriate technical and organisational security measures under Article 32 GDPR, pointing to basic security deficiencies at the processor including known unpatched vulnerabilities and lack of pre-incident encryption for phone numbers. The AEPD imposed an administrative fine of EUR 400,000 on Vodafone España.

Vodafone España notified the AEPD of a personal data breach originating from a cyberattack on a processor that provided software services for its Super Wifi 5 application. The incident exposed personal data of Vodafone customers, including email addresses and names. The AEPD found that Vodafone breached the confidentiality principle, failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures, and engaged the processor without a valid data processing agreement in place at the time of the breach. The authority imposed three administrative fines totaling €750,000.

Vodafone España notified the Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) of a ransomware attack affecting an IT system managed by a data processor, which compromised personal data of 724,733 customers. Although proceedings were initiated for alleged violations of both Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR, the AEPD determined that all facts constituted a single infringement of Article 32 GDPR due to basic security deficiencies. Taking into account aggravating factors such as the number of affected individuals, serious negligence, previous sanctions, and the nature of the business, alongside post-breach mitigation measures as an attenuating factor, the AEPD imposed an administrative fine of €500,000.

The Spanish DPA examined 191 complaints (162 after leaving out 29 with faulty data) about marketing calls, SMS and emails made on behalf of Vodafone España, including to people who had opted out or were on advertising exclusion (Robinson) lists. It found that Vodafone failed to control its processors (Arts. 28 and 24 GDPR), made international transfers in breach of Art. 44 GDPR, breached Art. 21 LSSICE on commercial electronic communications, and breached Art. 48.1.b LGT read with Art. 21 GDPR and Art. 23 LOPDGDD on the right to object to unwanted calls. It imposed four fines (EUR 4,000,000, 2,000,000, 150,000 and 2,000,000, EUR 8,150,000 in total) and ordered Vodafone to bring its processing into line with the GDPR and LOPDGDD within six months.

A former customer complained that a CaixaBank group consumer finance entity had queried solvency files about him and included him in a pre-approved credit campaign although he was no longer a customer. The AEPD opened investigations into how the entity profiles customers for commercial purposes. It found that the consent-gathering procedures for profiling lacked a valid legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR. It fined CaixaBank Payments & Consumer EUR 3,000,000 and ordered it to bring its consent procedures for commercial profiling into line with data protection law within six months.

The DPA fined a controller €280,000 for sending marketing emails to a user who had never confirmed their sign-up. Without that confirmation, no contract existed and Article 6(1)(b) GDPR could not apply.

The Hellenic DPA (HDPA) fined a politician €1000 for unsolicited political communication (SMS) without consent or any other legal basis, according to the national provisions on unsolicited communications.

The Hellenic DPA (HDPA) fined a politician €2000 for unsolicited political communication (email) without consent or any other legal basis according to the national provisions on unsolicited communications.
The Hamburg DPA fined Vattenfall Europe, an energy provider, €901,388 for violating Articles 12 and 13 GDPR by not informing their customers of data reconciliation sufficiently.

The UK DPA fined a controller approximately €200,000 (£170,000) for contacting almost 200,000 individuals who had registered their intent not to receive marketing calls with the Telephone Preference Service ('TPS'). In particular, the controller had failed to check datasets purchased from 11 third-party data providers against the TPS.

<!--Here the main article starts--> The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) decided not to take further actions over the Department for Digital, Culture, Media & Sport (DCMS) for its management of a UK citizen's (the complainant) request of information on which articles of the (now repealed) Directive 95/46/EC, according to the European Commission, had not been properly implemented by the UK government at the (now repealed) Data Protection Act 1998.

<!--Here the main article starts--> On 6 February 2020, ICO adopted a decision, stating that the Northamptonshire Police acted lawfully by refusing to confirm or deny whether it held information requested by the complainant. However, ICO found that the Northamptonshire Police’s failure to specify the exemption on which it was relying constituted a breach. These conclusions were made based on the relevant provisions of the Freedom of Information Act 2000 ("FOIA"), Data Protection Act 2018 and the General Data Protection regulation ("GDPR").

The DPA fined a company €5,320 for a failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures in connection with the destruction of employees' personal data contained in paper documents. Discarded documents were left unsecured and accessible to anyone.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued an opinion that employers cannot collect or process employee's COVID-19 test results or their health card number unless required to do so by sectoral regulation. Even where such regulations are in place, the employer must prove that their data collection practices comply with the principle of data minimization.

The Slovenian DPA issued an advisory opinion on the establishment of a temporary information system for the combat against the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic to the government of the Republic of Slovenia and the Jozef Stefan Institute.
The Slovenian DPA stated that it is allowed to make public only those minutes of the parent council meetings that contain public information.

<!--Here the main article starts--> On 14 February the Informacijski pooblaščenec of the Republic of Slovenia (IP), provided a non-binding opinion pursuant to Article 58(3) GDPR. The IP pronounced itself on the use of drones.

<!--Here the main article starts--> The Informacijski pooblaščenec, Information Commissioner of the Republic of Slovenia (IP), provided an opinion pursuant to Article 58 GDPR. The subject matter of the opinion regarded processing of personal data in an employment context.

<!--Here the main article starts--> On 14 February the Informacijski pooblaščenec, Information Commissioner of the Republic of Slovenia (IP), provided a non-binding opinion pursuant to Article 58 GDPR. The subject matter of the opinion regarded the legality of installing an automatic camera for the purpose of monitoring recreational activities on watercourses in the Triglay National Park (TNP). The IP refrained from commenting in the particular, but highlighted areas which required a closer look by the park.
The Slovenian DPA stated that the director (CEO) or member of the management of the company shall not be a DPO.

The DPA held that the Farmers’ Association published data concerning registration and ownership of horses in a public database and lawfully licensed this data to the provider of an app for horse owners. According to the DPA, this was necessary for the public interest.

The DPA issued a reprimand against an employee of a hospital for conducting unauthorised searches of a data subjects medical records. The DPA considered the employee to be a controller because they exceeded their access rights.
The DPA reprimanded an airport operator for informing data subjects inadequately and too late about the usage of CCTV and licence plate monitoring in its airport car parks.

The Icelandic DPA (Persónuvernd) has ruled that the National Commissioner of Police had been allowed to refuse to give information about which employees looked up complainant's personal data in the case file system, LÖKE. However, the Commissioner was requested to provide information about which responsible parties were looking for complainant's personal data.

The Icelandic DPA issued an advisory opinion clarifying the interplay between the Information Act and the Privacy Act which implements the GDPR in Iceland. The DPA clarified that the information in question is personal data and that processing of personal data requires a legal ground as per Article 6 GDPR.

<!--Here the main article starts--> Persónuvernd decided on a case concerning a list of employee’s sick leave put up in a hotel kitchen. A list of absences was hung up in a space accessible to all of the hotel’s employees. While the registration of sick leave was covered by sectorial labor law, and thus had a legal basis under Article 9 GDPR, the security of processing was not ensured following Article 5 (1)(f).

<!--Here the main article starts--> A person filed a complaint with the Finnish Data Protection Authority (Tietosuojavaltuutetun toimisto) regarding not being notified that a sales call had been recorded and being denied access to recording of the call. The Tietosuojavaltuutetun toimisto found that the company’s procedure to record calls did not fulfil the requirements under Article 5(1)(a), 12(1) and 13 GDPR. The decision highlighted that audio is personal data when it is stored and it is possible to identify an individual. As such, companies must inform data subjects when they collect the information. In addition, data subjects have the right to receive a copy of the call. The Data Protection Authority therefore ordered the company to modify its processing operation pursuant to Article 58(2)(d) GDPR.

The Data Protection Authority of Finland instructed a debt collection agency to delete personal data pursuant to the request of the data subject. According to applicable obligations arising from the Finnish Accounting Act, the personal data concerned should not to be retained.

The Court upheld the decision of the Municipal Court, which clarified that data subjects do not have legal standing to challenge the outcome of administrative proceedings, however may challenge DPA’s decisions which concern their specific complaints.
